Canyon Creatures

From a research ship off the coast of Argentina, Daniel Lauretta watched a robot sink into the ocean. The robot was named SuBastian. It was a remotely operated vehicle. SuBastian was carrying cameras to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean’s Mar del Plata Canyon. The underwater valley is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.

When SuBastian got to the seafloor, Lauretta worried. “The first thing I saw, once the cameras reached the bottom, was just soft sediment,” he told TIME for Kids. “There were very few animals.”

There was no need to worry. Over 21 days in summer 2025, SuBastian dove 17 times. It found coral reefs. It found sea stars. It found animals no person had ever seen. About a year later, a team of scientists examined the mission’s findings. In September, the team announced that it identified 57 never-seen marine species.

Live From the Deep

Lauretta is a researcher at the Argentine Museum of Natural Sciences. That’s in Buenos Aires. He led the expedition’s science team, which was run by the Schmidt Ocean Institute. As Lauretta watched SuBastian explore, the cameras streamed live video online. Millions of people tuned in.

Suddenly, an orange sea star came into view. Viewers thought it looked like a character from SpongeBob SquarePants. “The chat exploded with comments about its resemblance to Patrick Star,” Lauretta says. The sea star became famous. It was not a new species. The scientists left it where it was. But the team collected other animals from the canyon and took them to the lab. That’s where the real discoveries began.

Species Detectives

In July 2026, 20 taxonomists and other researchers gathered in Buenos Aires for two weeks to study the animals from the canyon. They would figure out which ones were new to science. “It’s like being a detective,” says Francisco Solís-Marín. He’s a sea cucumber expert. To learn whether an animal is a new discovery, he compares its shape and body parts to those of every known species.

One newly discovered sea cucumber is about four inches long. It’s almost transparent. It has bumps that look like horns. The team called it Loki. That’s a Marvel character who wears a horned helmet (see “What’s in a Name?”). “Sea cucumbers are some of the ocean’s little superheroes,” Solís-Marín says. “Some can swim, glow, or defend themselves in amazing ways.”

The smallest discoveries came from mud: Copepods are crustaceans. They’re smaller than a grain of rice. Scientists examined only a 10th of the copepod samples. Each was a new species. “There is still a whole new world to discover,” says Emanuel Pereira, a copepod scientist. Lauretta’s team is heading back in early 2027. They’ll explore a different canyon. “I hope to find many new species,” he says.

What’s in a Name?

Loki is a nickname. But every newly discovered species needs an official scientific name. To choose it, scientists write a report. They describe how the animal is different from known species. It can take months or years to complete this process. But there’s a reward: “As the scientists studying this new species, we get to choose its official name,” Solís-Marín says. Until then, Loki officially goes by Peniagone sp. The sp. means the species hasn’t yet been named.
